extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Montaigne / readers of Renaissance essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / interpretation of Montaigne's essay 'Upon Some Verses of Virgil' (reflections on age, pleasure, marriage, honesty, and moderation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in serious meditation
rubrics_metrics.description: A man should have his soul instructed in the means to sustain and to contend with evils, and often rouse it up and exercise it in this noble study; but in an ordinary soul it must be by intervals and with moderation;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that continual intent upon grave matters (vice, death, poverty, disease) will besot the mind; such meditations are profitable and solid but also cumbersome and heavy, so they should be practised intermittently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes of temperance or pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Wisdom has its excesses, and has no less need of moderation than folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author resists both unbridled pleasure and over-strict temperance (which can lead to stupidity); he deliberately allows small youthful diversions to prevent drying up under excessive prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match disposition to practice (body-mind correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: This body of mine avoids disorder and dreads it; 'tis now my body's turn to guide my mind towards reformation; it governs ... and is always preaching to me death, patience, and repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne emphasizes that bodily condition affects mental life: health and age shape temperament and capacities; practices (like recreation or study) should account for that relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gaiety to temper sourness of character
rubrics_metrics.description: I love a gay and civil wisdom, and fly from all sourness and austerity of manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He prefers pleasant, civil conduct to stern or repellent demeanour; virtue should be pleasant and not austere; sourness hides no real moral superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confess and study one's vices to correct them
rubrics_metrics.description: A man must see and study his vice to correct it; they who conceal it from others, commonly conceal it from themselves;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne claims that public (or at least acknowledged) confession helps make vice visible and thus correctable; concealment fosters self-deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness in confession compensates wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: The boldness of doing ill is in some sort compensated and restrained by the boldness of confessing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He suggests moral credit in owning one's faults: those who will tell all should be those who do nothing that they must hide; confession can sometimes satisfy or temper guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying is a worse fault than many private sins
rubrics_metrics.description: I look upon lying as a worse fault than [adultery].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne prefers candid admission of faults over deceit; he cites Thales' contrasting counsel but rejects shielding a greater wrong with a lesser lie.

rubrics_metrics.name: External decency should not cover inner vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward decency should not palliate vice: this rough-cast only appertains to a good and sound wall, that deserves to be preserved and whited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author condemns using ceremony or respectable appearance to hide immoral behaviour; genuine goodness should not be a mere façade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer being truly known to being falsely praised
rubrics_metrics.description: I am greedy of making myself known... I care not to how many, provided it be truly; or to say better, I hunger for nothing; but I mortally hate to be mistaken by those who happen to learn my name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic reputation (accurate knowledge of one's character) is valued over empty honour or praise that misrepresents who one is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive anticipation of future evils
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis great folly to lengthen and anticipate human incommodities, as every one does; I had rather be a less while old than be old before I am really so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mentally pre-age or pre-suffer; live in present opportunities and take small pleasures to offset melancholic anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, private pleasures over pompous display
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is a quality of very little ambition; it ... is best pleased where most retired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne favors modest, intimate pleasures (sweet, facile, ready) rather than grand, ostentatious pleasures tied to reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage should resemble friendship, not be confused with erotic love
rubrics_metrics.description: A good marriage... rejects the company and conditions of love, and tries to represent those of friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argues marriage's virtues are constancy, trust, mutual services and utility; conflating marriage with passionate love confuses distinct ends and weakens both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose marriage for more lasting foundations than beauty or passion
rubrics_metrics.description: I see no marriages where the conjugal compatibility sooner fails than those that we contract upon the account of beauty and amorous desires; there should be more solid and constant foundation, and they should proceed with greater circumspection;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence and circumspection (considering family, posterity, interest) are better bases for marriage than transient attractions of beauty or desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrain liberty prudently once obligations are assumed
rubrics_metrics.description: A man must prudently manage his liberty; but having once submitted to obligation, he must confine himself within the laws of common duty, at least, do what he can towards it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one enters social bonds (e.g., marriage or service), one should accept the limits and duties entailed rather than acting in deliberate contempt of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make virtue a sour, repellent affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: I hate a froward and dismal spirit, that slips over all the pleasures of life and seizes and feeds upon misfortunes... Virtue is a pleasant and gay quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises those who display virtue as sternness or morbidity; genuine virtue is compatible with cheerfulness and sociability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the bodily sources of mental enthusiasms and declines
rubrics_metrics.description: Our masters... have not also attributed a part [of extraordinary emotions] to health: a boiling, vigorous, full, and lazy health ... supplied me withal; that fire of sprightliness and gaiety darts into the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He reminds readers that bodily health supplies much of our mental liveliness (poesy, love, wine effects), and conversely bodily decline stupefies spirit; so evaluate mental states with reference to physical condition.
